- Pedregosa, F. m.fl. 2011. Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python. *Journal of Machine Learning Research* 12, s. 2825–2830.
- Platt, J. 1999. Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods. I: Smola, A. m.fl. (red.), *Advances in Large Margin Classifiers*. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, s. 61–74.
- Assael, Y., Sommerschield, T., Shillingford, B. m.fl. 2022. Restoring and attributing ancient texts using deep neural networks. *Nature* 603, s. 280–283.
posts.title_en: The missing runes – work in progress on Vitki's probability model
posts.summary_en: Many runestones have places where runes have been lost. We are building a model that proposes what stood there and says how sure it is. Here we report how far we have come and how the model is tested: six tests with a known answer, calibrated percentages and checks of the code. The model is not yet released in the app.
posts.body_en:
![Sö 45 in raking light, with a close-up of the damaged runes](/figurer/3125616ecf0efe16.webp)
Sö 45 at Stora Släbro in Södermanland, in raking light from a 3D scan. On the right, a close-up of the left rune band. Inside the dashed ring two runes are damaged in the stone's first word, the man's name GæiRf[as]tr: one by flint, the other by a deep pit. The image is computed in Vitki from Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt's scan (Swedish National Heritage Board, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), doi:[10.5281/zenodo.11951255](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11951255)).

Hardly any runestone has survived a thousand years undamaged. Stones have cracked, flakes have come off and weathering has eaten into the carving. Of the 2,633 Viking-age runestones in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base, 1,087 have at least one place where one to four runes have been lost.

When runologists publish a stone they often fill such gaps. The restored runes are put in square brackets, as in GæiRf[as]tr. The brackets say that the runes cannot be seen on the stone. They do not say how sure the editor was, or which other possibilities were weighed.

In Vitki we are building a model that does the same work in a different way. It proposes what stood in the gap, ranks the proposals and states how sure it is. The percentage is tested against gaps where the answer is known, so that 90 per cent should mean that the proposal is right about nine times out of ten. Here we report how far we have come, and we account for every test, so that anyone who wishes can examine how the model is built and tested before it is released.

:::box Work in progress
- The model is part of Vitki's open source code but is **not yet released in the app**. We are still testing and improving it.
- The figures apply to the version we have today (textmodel-18, October 2026) and may change.
- The figures apply to runestones, fragments and lost stones included. The model also reads inscriptions on other stones and loose objects such as amulets and rune bones, and where it does we say so.
- The proposals are proposals, not interpretations. The model works with runes, words and word order, not with what a text means.
:::

## A puzzle with too few pieces

The younger futhark has only 16 runes, but the language had many more sounds. The same rune therefore had to stand for several sounds: ᚴ could be k, g or ng, and ᛁ could be i, e, æ or j. Nor did the carvers always put dividers between the words. A sequence of runes can thus be read in several ways even when all the runes survive. When some are missing, the possibilities multiply.

![One rune – several sounds](/figurer/29d1d65f62c923ff.webp)
A selection from the model's spelling table, simplified. The model has learned how often each sound was written with each rune, in different periods and regions.

## How the model reasons

Take Sö 45 as an example. According to *Södermanlands runinskrifter* the stone is broken into three pieces. The first name begins with the runes kai on the lowest piece and continues with Rfastr on the upper left one. There the stave of the a is "indistinct because of flint", and of the s only "the upper stave and the starting point of the middle stroke" remain; "the rest of the rune is destroyed by a deep pit". The editors read GæiRf[as]tr. The model is shown the runes kaiRf??tr, where the two question marks are the lost runes.

![How the model reasons](/figurer/7380bef0a873dfc4.webp)
The model's steps, with the gap on Sö 45 as the example.

First the model tries which words can be spelled with the surviving runes plus two more. Then each proposal is weighed by how well it fits where it stands. It is the same principle as when a phone suggests the next word: some words tend to follow certain others. Here the word stands first in the text, followed by another name, Æistfari, and the verb *ræisþu*, 'raised'. The name GæiRfastr occurs on several other stones, for example Sö 227, Sm 111 and U 1144, so the model knows it. We did not enter any traces of the runes here.

The answer is GæiRfastr with 95 per cent and GæiRfriðr with 1. The first proposal is the same name that the editors wrote in. The model has not seen the text of Sö 45 itself, because a stone is always read by a version of the model that was trained without it.

## The building blocks

The model is not one big machine but several parts, each of which can be tested on its own. Several of them are well-tried methods from language technology. The model learns the language from every kind of Viking-age inscription, not only the runestones, since it is the same on an amulet as on a stone.

- **Spelling.** The model has learned how sounds were written in runes from 27,218 pairs of carved words and their normalized form, from 2,877 inscriptions. Spelling is estimated for each period and region, so that a stone from the 900s is not read like one from the 1000s.
- **Word order.** How often one word follows another is counted with a method from speech recognition, Kneser–Ney smoothing (Kneser & Ney 1995). It also gives rare word pairs a reasonable chance.
- **Word classes.** Words that occur in similar contexts are grouped automatically. The genitives *hans*, *hennaR*, *sina* and *þæiRa* end up in the same class without anyone having told the model what a genitive is. This helps it with rare words. The classes are computed with scikit-learn.
- **Names.** Many names occur on one stone only. The model therefore builds unknown names from first elements, second elements and endings, spelled as the carvers spelled them. The first element Ragn-, for example, is carved as *rahn* 17 times in Rundata.
- **Neighbouring stones.** Names on stones within ten kilometres weigh a little more, since the same families often raised several stones in the same district.
- **Dividers.** Carvers differed. Most put dividers between nearly all words, some between none at all. The model therefore estimates for each stone how often that carver marked a word boundary, and lets this decide how readily it places a boundary itself where the carver put no sign.
- **Traces.** If a remnant of a rune is visible in the scan or in the edition's description, it can be entered. A trace counts as likely but not certain, so that a misread remnant does not shut out the right answer.
- **Calibration.** The model's own percentages were too high, especially for names. They are therefore adjusted with a logistic model, the same principle as in Platt (1999), separately for formula words, known names, names the model has composed itself and other words. All the proposals in a gap are calibrated together, and "none of the proposals" gets a probability of its own; the first choice gets a deduction of its own, since it was chosen precisely because its probability was the highest. The calibration is estimated on three kinds of gaps with a known answer, described below.
- **No cheating.** The material is split into five parts by signum. A stone is always read by a model trained on the other four, so that the editors' restoration never leaks in. When a single stone is to be analysed, the model can also be trained on everything except that stone.

## Six tests with a known answer

A proposal is only worth something if you know how often it is right. We therefore test the model in six ways, always on stones it was not trained on. Each test answers a question of its own:

- **The reading test:** does the model read whole texts correctly when it must decide for itself where the words begin?
- **The masking test:** can it fill runes that we hide in texts with a known answer?
- **The hard masking test:** can it do the same when the answer is never a formula word?
- **The editors' gaps:** does it arrive at the same word as the editors where they have filled a gap?
- **The documented gaps:** is it right where runes have really been lost but are known from older drawings?
- **The dating test:** can it tell when a text was written, from the language alone?

:::chart Right word in the tests, runestones
+The reading test | 85.2 | 9,159 words on 698 runestones
Masking, inside a word | 75.5 | 698 gaps
Masking, whole word | 58.7 | 698 gaps
Masking, whole word with half the rune visible | 84.2 | simulated traces
Hard masking, inside a word | 47.1 | 698 gaps without formula words
The editors' gaps | 85.5 | 544 gaps
Documented gaps | 69.0 | 361 gaps
Source: Vitki's tests with textmodel-18, in five parts. The tests measure different things and are hard in different ways, so the bars should not be compared as a contest.
:::

**The reading test.** The model reads 808 inscriptions where the answer is known, 10,669 words in all, without the editors' word boundaries. It chooses the same word as the editors in 84.3 per cent of cases and divides the words correctly in 94.6 per cent. When the first version was ready in October the figures were 81 and 92 per cent. Three percentage points may sound little, but it is about 300 more words read correctly, and about half of the gain came when the model learned to build names. The 808 inscriptions are 698 runestones, 84 other stones and 26 loose objects. On the runestones the model chooses the same word as the editors in 85.2 per cent of cases and divides the words correctly in 95.4 per cent. The loose objects are hardest, at 56 and 71 per cent.

:::chart The reading test, from the first version to today
# Same word as the editors
First version | 81
+Today | 84.3
# Words divided correctly
First version | 92
+Today | 94.6
Source: Vitki's reading test on 808 inscriptions (698 runestones, 84 other stones and 26 loose objects) with 10,669 words, in five parts.
:::

**The masking test.** Here we hide runes in texts where the answer is known and let the model fill them in. If a few runes inside a word on a runestone are missing, it gives the right word in 76 per cent of cases. If a whole word is missing, the figure is 59 per cent, since then no runes are left to go on, only the words around it. In a simulated test on runestones, where half of each lost rune is visible, the share of whole words that are right rises to 84 per cent, and it is still 77 per cent when one trace in five is misread. That test is simulated with clean rune shapes and shows what the traces are worth at best.

**The hard masking test.** Formula words such as *stone*, *raised* and *in memory of* are easy to guess. In this test we therefore hide only words outside the 50 most common. The model then gives the right word in 47 per cent of cases when a few runes are missing inside the word, and in 9 per cent when the whole word is missing. The test shows how much the formulas help, and how hard it is to guess an unusual word without traces. What matters is that the model knows it, and it does so almost all the way: when it says at least 95 per cent it is right in 96 cases out of a hundred here too, measured by the same rule as in the editors' gaps – counting every normalization variant as wrong instead, such as hakun against hakon, gives 92 out of a hundred. The test did teach us one reservation: in the 80–95 per cent band the model is somewhat too sure about unusual words. There it claims 89 per cent on average but is right in 84 cases out of a hundred. Anyone filling a gap whose answer cannot be a formula word should read percentages in that band with that margin.

**The editors' gaps.** We test the model on 565 gaps on 399 runestones that the editors have filled. The model makes a proposal in 544 of them, and 85 per cent of the proposals are the same word the editors chose. Formula words are right in 96 per cent, names in 75 and other words in 65 per cent. Even so, this test is easier than reality. Editors prefer to fill gaps where the answer is given and leave the hard ones open, so the gaps they have filled are often the simple ones.

**The documented gaps.** A better test is found in Rundata itself. Runes within square brackets are lost on the stone but known from older drawings. They fell off for physical reasons, not because they were easy to guess, and yet the answer is documented. We turn each such run of one to four runes inside a word into a gap. On 361 such gaps on runestones the model gives the right word in 69 per cent of cases. That is lower than in the other tests, as expected: here the gaps lie wherever the damage happened to fall, and the rest of the stone is often damaged too. It is the test that most resembles the gaps the model is meant for.

**The dating test.** The model can also estimate when a text was written, from its spelling and vocabulary. It reads the text with each of four periods, from the 800s to the 1100s, and chooses the one in which the text is most probable. On 1,670 dated runestones it chooses the right period in 59 per cent of cases. Always guessing the most common period gives 47 per cent. It is at most one period off in 95 per cent. That is not enough to replace the style groups, but it can give a first date to the stones that have none.

## When it says 90 per cent, it means 90 per cent

What matters most is not that the model is right as often as possible, but that its percentages can be trusted. A weather forecast that says 70 per cent chance of rain should see rain on about seven days out of ten. We hold the model to the same standard.

Here the documented gaps were decisive. With a calibration estimated on the editors' gaps alone, the percentages held there, but not on the documented gaps. When the model said about 62 per cent, it was right in only 33 per cent of cases. It was too sure precisely where the answer was uncertain. The calibration is now estimated on three kinds of gaps together: the editors' gaps, the masked words and the documented gaps. The app uses the level of the documented gaps, since they resemble real damage.

The calibration does more than adjust figures: the model now chooses the word with the highest calibrated percentage, not necessarily the language model's own first choice. A word's percentage can never overtake another word of the same class, but a formula word can overtake a composed name, since composed names are more often wrong. In cross-validated tests this choice raised the share of right words from 69.1 to 69.9 per cent on the documented gaps and from 85.5 to 85.7 on the editors' gaps.

:::chart What the model says and how often it is right, on the documented gaps
# The model says under 50 %
Says on average | 28
+Is right | 23 | 101 gaps
# The model says 50–80 %
Says on average | 65
+Is right | 52 | 44 gaps
# The model says 80–95 %
Says on average | 88
+Is right | 87 | 46 gaps
# The model says at least 95 %
Says on average | 99
+Is right | 99 | 165 gaps
Source: 361 documented gaps on runestones (runes known from older drawings). Each gap got its percentage from a calibration made without its stone.
:::

The bars in each pair should be equally long, and in three of the four bands they are. In the middle range, where the gaps are few, the model is still somewhat too sure. The average distance between what the model says and how often it is right, the measure called calibration error, fell on the documented gaps from 14.4 to 3.4 percentage points. When the model says at least 95 per cent it is right in 99 per cent of cases. That applies to 165 of the documented gaps.

We also tested the calibration where it had not seen the answers. In the hard masking test, which was not used when it was estimated, the calibration error for gaps inside a word fell from 17 to 4.8 percentage points. In the editors' gaps the model arrives at the same word as the editors in 99.6 per cent of the cases where it says at least 95 per cent. And in the reading test the model's own percentages for the words differed on average by 8.8 percentage points from how often it was actually right; after calibration the difference is 0.6 percentage points.

## Checked in detail

A tool meant for research must be trustworthy also in the parts one does not see. We have therefore checked the model's calculations against independent programs and against itself:

- **Word order** is computed exactly as in NLTK, a widely used library for language technology. The largest difference over 3,000 word pairs is 10⁻¹⁶, nothing but rounding.
- **The calibration** gives the same results as scikit-learn. We also tried another method, isotonic calibration, but it gave worse results and is not used.
- **The faster calculation.** For each proposal in a gap the model used to read the whole text again. Since a word never runs across a divider, it is enough to read the group around the gap again. The new calculation gives the same answers as the old one, with differences of at most 10⁻¹⁴, and is 4.7 times faster.
- **Stones with many gaps.** When the proposals for the gaps give more than 256 combinations, the model searches for the best one gap by gap. On U 512, with nine gaps, this gave the same answer as trying every combination.
- **Automatic tests.** 32 tests run at every change to the code.
- **Everything is open.** The code, the tests and the figures are on [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes), and the method is described in [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md), section 8.1.

## A blind test, locked in advance

Every figure above comes from tests we built and read off ourselves as the work went along. No test stone is ever part of its own model, but whoever builds a tool can still shape it, without noticing, after their test data. We therefore finished with a blind test under a pre-registered protocol. Population, drawing rule, settings, measures and pass limits were written down and locked in the version history before a single gap was filled, and the draw's random seed is the registration's own checksum – so the selection cannot have been picked after the fact. From 197 runestones with documented gaps, where every stone that had ever appeared in our articles, scans or case studies was removed in advance, 14 stones with 21 gaps were drawn. The locked requirement: between 10 and 18 right out of 21 would be consistent with the benchmark, the test runs once, and the result is reported whatever it shows.

The model chose the editors' word in 16 of 21 gaps, 76 per cent – in the middle of the locked interval. All 13 gaps where it claimed at least 95 per cent came out right. And four of the five misses carried the model's own warning, with claims below 45 per cent: *spaka* where the editors read the compound *malspaka*, guesses at 14 per cent where the answer is the place name *svanaby* and the rare name *liðsvaldr*. The one half-confident miss deserves quoting as it stands: in Sm 121's *---ur* the model proposed *faður*, "father", at 77 per cent – the editors read *moðurbroður*, "mother's brother". The protocol, the draw and every gap's outcome sit untouched in the version history on GitHub.

## Sö 206: a single rune decides

Sö 206 stands at Överselö church. Rundata translates the inscription: "Here shall these stones stand, reddened with runes: Guðlaug raised (them) in memory of her sons; and Hjalmlaug in memory of her brothers." Two places are damaged.

![Sö 206 with a close-up of the weathered band](/figurer/250d42fd64fd465e.webp)
Sö 206 at Överselö church, exported at high resolution from Vitki by Viktor Kvant. On the right, the top of the left rune band. The ring shows roughly where the lost rune of *ru?niR* was. The image is computed from Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt's scan (Swedish National Heritage Board, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), doi:[10.5281/zenodo.11951255](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11951255)).

In the first word, *ru?niR*, the rune is according to the edition "entirely gone, because a flake of the stone surface has fallen off". The model has two main proposals: *Hrungnir*, the name of a giant in the Edda, and *roðnir*, 'reddened', which is the editors' reading. The language model itself prefers the giant, with 60 per cent against 27. But in tests with a known answer such first choices often prove wrong, and after calibration 26 per cent remain for *Hrungnir* and 18 for *roðnir* – the rest is left open. The language alone thus does not settle the matter.

The difference between the proposals is a single rune. *roðnir* is written with þ and *Hrungnir* with k, *rukniR*. Had the scan shown a remnant of one or the other, the question would be nearly settled.

![A single trace decides](/figurer/96c76883fac94e99.webp)
The model's proposals for *ru?niR* on Sö 206, without a trace and with an imagined trace of þ or k. Traces count as likely, not certain, which is why no proposal reaches 100 per cent.

On Sö 206 there is no such remnant, since the flake is gone. The editors instead settled the matter by meaning. Elias Wessén writes in the edition that it is "not possible, by inserting any rune other than þ, to obtain a word that makes sense in the context". He mentions that Hallström had objected to the reading in Fornvännen in 1931, but dismisses the objections as "a scepticism carried too far". The model works with words and word order, not with meaning. What it adds is to show exactly what the decision rests on: a single rune, and the meaning.

In the second damaged word, *k???auk*, only the lower parts of the staves of three runes remain according to the edition, "but the reading is certain because of Sö 208". On that stone, at the same church, Guðlaug and Hjalmlaug stand together. Sö 208 is in the same test part as Sö 206, and so the ordinary model has not seen it. It gives no proposal more than 11 per cent: *Guðlaug* 11, *Gíslaug* 8 and *kumbl* 6 per cent. In other words, it says that it does not know. When a single stone is to be analysed for real, the model is therefore trained on everything except that stone, so that it sees the sister stones but never the stone's own text.

:::box More scanned stones from the same series
- **Sö 137, Aspa:** *þ??si* becomes *þannsi*, 'this', with 97.4 per cent. The editors read þ[ann]si.
- **Sö 211, Ljunga:** *sta??* becomes *stæin*, 'stone', with 99.9 per cent. The editors read stæ[in].
- Formula words like these are the easiest gaps. Names are harder: in *hak????* on Sö 211, where the editors read Hak[i ok], the model gives no proposal above 23 per cent.
:::

## Every runestone with gaps

We let the model read all 1,087 Viking-age runestones that have gaps of one to four runes. 58 of them have fewer than four legible runes and cannot be read. The other 1,029, with 1,910 gaps in all, are read in five parts at once on an ordinary computer, and the run takes about 25 minutes. The first run took considerably longer; the faster calculation above has shortened it. At the same time the model read 247 inscriptions on other stones and loose objects, with 476 gaps, but we do not count them here.

:::chart How sure the model is in all 1,910 gaps on the runestones
+At least 95 % | 17.5 | 335 gaps
80–95 % | 10.4 | 199 gaps
50–80 % | 14.9 | 284 gaps
Under 50 % | 56.5 | 1,079 gaps
No proposal | 0.7 | 13 gaps where the word is unknown to the model
Source: Vitki's run of textmodel-18 on every Viking-age runestone in Rundata with gaps of 1–4 runes, fragments and lost stones included.
:::

In 18 per cent of the gaps the model is at least 95 per cent sure. In 56 per cent it is under 50 per cent, and there it gives a list of several proposals instead of an answer.

Most interesting is the comparison with the editors. Among the gaps on Swedish runestones that the editors have filled, the model says at least 95 per cent in 267 of 555. Among those the editors left open, it does so in none of the 70. Where the runologists could not settle the matter, the model thus never claims to know. That is how we want it to work.

In 108 gaps the words stand without dividers, and the proposal changes if the words are divided as the editors divide them. There the model shows both proposals.

## Why it matters

- **The certainty is visible.** A square bracket shows that something is restored. The model also shows how certain it is and which other possibilities exist, with percentages tested against the answer.
- **The same yardstick for every stone.** All 1,910 gaps on the runestones are read by the same rules. When the model improves, or a new reading appears, everything can be recalculated.
- **It shows where to look.** On Sö 206 everything depends on whether a remnant of þ or k survives. With 3D scans such places can be examined to half a millimetre.
- **Everything is open.** The code, the tests and the figures are on [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes), so that anyone can test them again.

Similar tools have been built for Greek inscriptions, where the model Ithaca proposes lost letters (Assael et al. 2022). Vitki's model is built for the runes' own difficulties: the ambiguous spelling, the many names and the traces in the scans. It does not replace the runologist. It gives the runologist a second opinion that can be counted on.

## Before the model is released

Work remains before the model comes out in the app:

- **Traces from the scans.** Today the model only counts traces that someone has entered by hand, but the reader that will take them straight from the 3D scan is well under way. The branches, which tell the runes apart, cannot be trusted in the thinned groove lines – they are now read from the depth image itself instead, weighted by how deeply they are carved. In a first test on 17 scanned stones, where whole words were masked and filled by a model that had never seen the stone, the share right rose from 53.5 to 59.9 per cent when the scanner's traces were allowed to help – and with the traces randomly reshuffled among the stone's runes the whole gain vanished. So it is the stone that is being read, not an exercise in numbers. At badly weathered patches the traces can mislead, so the panel shows what the scanner sees – the branches with their carving depth and the possible runes – and the traces only count once the user has confirmed them. A rune with more deep branches than any rune holds, a possible bind rune, proposes nothing at all.
- **Names.** Names are right in 75 per cent of the editors' gaps, against 96 for formula words. Most errors in the documented gaps concern names. The latest version took a step right here: the name builder's proposals used to be cut from the candidate list before they could be weighed, and when they were given a place of their own (textmodel-18) the model won eight masked gaps – among them the names *Guðfastr* and *Þormóðr* – without losing any.
- **More texts from Denmark and Norway**, so that the yardstick is equally fair to every country.
- **Inflection.** The model does not know case and agreement. That concerns only about one word in a hundred in the reading test, however, mostly names in the wrong case. Most of what looks like a wrong form is instead different normalizations in Rundata, such as *sin* and *sinn*.
- **The answer key.** The editors' restoration is itself a judgement. The masking test and the documented gaps have a firmer answer.

When this is in place, the model will come out in the panel *Reading and gaps* on every inscription's page in Vitki.

## The other model: how language-like is a sequence of runes?

Vitki also has a smaller model that measures how much a sequence of runes resembles language. We used it in the article [Interpret, he who can](/artiklar/hur-spraklik-ar-en-runfoljd) to divide the uninterpreted inscriptions into futhark rows, broken language and sequences that do not resemble language. It too has been improved by tests that first went wrong. Short, broken pieces looked incomprehensible just because they were short, so each inscription is now compared with real texts cut to exactly the same lengths. Danish and Norwegian fragments were at first measured against a mostly Swedish yardstick; now they are compared with texts from the same country. The futhark row on DR EM85;470C, *fuþrkhainsl*, was first judged "not language" because it departs from the usual order; now futhark rows with deviations are recognised too. And Rundata's alternative readings are no longer counted as part of the text. Every change is in the code.

## How we did it

- **Data:** the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (Rundata). The model learns from all 3,662 Viking-age inscriptions with transliteration and normalization and from the vocabulary of the Edda. The tests and the run are reported for the 2,633 runestones, fragments and lost stones included. Other stones and loose objects are named separately (utdata/modellartikel/runstenar.py).
- **The reading test:** scripts/runlm_calibrate.py, on 808 inscriptions where Rundata's words cover the carved text exactly. The material is split into five parts by signum.
- **The masking tests:** scripts/runlm_restore_test.py, 1396 hidden gaps on runestones, and with --hard only words outside the 50 most common. The traces in the simulated test are drawn with the typeface Apple Symbols.
- **The editors' gaps:** scripts/runlm_gaps.py. The same word in another inflection or normalization counts as the same word.
- **The documented gaps:** scripts/runlm_documented_test.py. Runes within square brackets are turned into gaps, and the answer is the documented runes and Rundata's normalization.
- **The calibration:** scripts/runlm_gap_calibrate.py, with all three kinds of gaps and cross-validation with whole stones held out.
- **The dating test:** scripts/runlm_dating.py, on 1,670 dated runestones.
- **The run over every stone:** scripts/textmodel_batch.py. The comparison with the editors is made in utdata/modellartikel/batch_status.py.
- **Sö 206 with traces:** the model's answer when only þ, or only k, is allowed in the gap (src/textmodel.py, with traces counted as likely).
- **The images:** Sö 45 in raking light, computed in Vitki. Sö 206 exported at high resolution from Vitki. The illustrations are drawn with utdata/modellartikel/figurer.py.
- **The whole method:** [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md), section 8.1.

## About the scans

Sö 45 and Sö 206 were scanned by Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt of the Swedish National Heritage Board within the research project Runristandets dynamik (2009–2014), with a scanner that measures the surface with structured light. Only the carved surfaces were scanned. In 2024 she published the scans of 35 runestones from Södermanland openly on Zenodo, under the licence CC BY 4.0. We use the files *So 45_1_4 thin_closed holes.stl* and *So 206_thin03_closed holes.stl* as published. The image of Sö 45 is computed in Vitki, and the image of Sö 206 was exported at high resolution from Vitki by Viktor Kvant. Her own studies of the scans are Kitzler Åhfeldt 2015 and 2017. We are grateful that the dataset has been made freely available.

:::box The essentials in brief
- We are building a model that reads the runestone texts and proposes words for lost runes – without ever having seen the interpretation of the stone it reads.
- The most important figure is not how often the model is right, but that it knows when it is unsure: when it claims at least 95 per cent, the word is almost always right, tested in a pre-registered blind test.
- On the hardest gaps – where the runes are truly lost but the answer is known from older drawings – it picks the right word in about seven cases out of ten. That is enough to be a real help with damaged stones, but not to replace the runologist's judgement – and that is how the figures should be read.
- Traces in the 3D scans lift the reading further, and everything is shown openly in the app: proposals, percentages and alternatives. The model is a tool that declares its own uncertainty, not an oracle.
:::

## Sources

- Kitzler Åhfeldt, L. 2015. Rune Carvers and Local Mobility. *Viking and Medieval Scandinavia* 11, pp. 143–182.
- Kitzler Åhfeldt, L. 2017. *Runristare och mobilitet i Södermanland*. Report. Stockholm: Swedish National Heritage Board.
- The Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (Rundata), Department of Scandinavian Languages, Uppsala University. Open Database License.
- Brate, E. & Wessén, E. 1924–36. *Södermanlands runinskrifter* (Sveriges runinskrifter 3). Stockholm: KVHAA. Digitized by the [Swedish National Heritage Board](https://www.raa.se/kulturarv/runor-och-runstenar/digitala-sveriges-runinskrifter/). Sö 45 on pp. 34 f., Sö 206 and Sö 208 on pp. 181 ff.
- Kneser, R. & Ney, H. 1995. Improved backing-off for M-gram language modeling. *Proceedings of the 1995 International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing* 1, pp. 181–184.

posts.title: Stilgruppernas mörkertal
posts.summary: Runstenarna dateras med sina ornament, men mer än var tredje runsten saknar stilgrupp i Samnordisk runtextdatabas – och bortfallet är inte slumpmässigt. De skadade, de otolkade och stenarna utanför Mälardalen och Västergötland försvinner oftast. Vi visar att de osynliga stenarna inte heller beter sig som de synliga, att kategorin RAK gör hela bestånd tidiga per definition, och hur mörkertalet kan tändas.
posts.body:
När Anne-Sofie Gräslund delade in runstenarna efter runbandens och djurornamentikens form fick forskningen sitt kanske vassaste verktyg: en runsten kan dateras på några decenniers när, utan ett enda årtal i texten. Stilgrupperna bär i dag stora delar av vad vi tror oss veta om vikingatidens slut – när ristarna började signera, när bönerna kom, hur korset spred sig.

Men ett verktyg ser bara det som ligger i dess ljus. Den här artikeln ställer frågan som sällan ställs: vilka runstenar ser stilgrupperna – och vilka står i mörkret? Svaret är att mer än var tredje runsten saknar stilgrupp i Samnordisk runtextdatabas, och att bortfallet inte är slumpmässigt. De stenar som saknas är systematiskt de skadade, de otolkade och de perifera. Och de beter sig inte som de synliga.

:::box I korthet
- Av 2 633 vikingatida runstenar har 1 701 en stilgrupp i Samnordisk runtextdatabas. Drygt nio hundra, 35 procent, står utanför.
- Bortfallet följer skadan: en hel svensk runsten har stilgrupp i 83 fall av hundra, en med förlorade runor i 54. Att en så stor skillnad skulle uppstå av slump är i praktiken uteslutet.
- Det följer också tolkningen och geografin: de otolkade runstenarna har stilgrupp i 46 fall av hundra mot de tolkades 73, och Öland, Gotland och Småland ligger under hälften.
- De osynliga stenarna är inte som de synliga: hela runstenar utan stilgrupp är signerade i 6 fall av hundra, mot 16 bland de stilsatta – de signerar som den äldsta stilgruppen.
- Kategorin RAK definieras av något som saknas. Bland Danmarks stilsatta runstenar är 95 av hundra RAK, bland Norges alla, i Uppland 6 av hundra. Läst som datering blir hela länder tidiga per definition.
- Mörkertalet kan tändas: en seriation daterar 317 av Upplands 374 runstenar utan stilgrupp, och textmodellen prickar rätt århundrade för 58,5 procent av runstenarna i korsvaliderade prov.
:::

## Verktyget som daterar djuren

Gräslunds system går från RAK, där runbandet har raka ändar utan djurhuvud, över fågelperspektivets Fp och korsbandsstilens KB till profilstilarna Pr1–Pr5, där djuret ses från sidan och blir allt smalare och mer utdraget. Ordningen är prövad mot myntdaterade depåer och mot stenarnas inbördes hänvisningar, och den håller: när vi själva seriationsprövar Upplands runstenar, som vi visar längre ned, följer textens och innehållets drag Gräslunds ordning med god marginal. Inget i den här artikeln ifrågasätter systemet. Frågan är vad systemet inte ser.

![Runstenen U 142 vid Fällbro](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg/960px-Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg)
U 142 vid Fällbro i Täby, i profilstilen Pr4 och signerad av Öpir. Runbandets djur, med huvudet i profil, är själva dateringsunderlaget. Foto: Potatisodlarn, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg).

## Vem som står i mörkret

:::chart Andel runstenar med stilgrupp i Samnordisk runtextdatabas
# Efter land
Danmark | 80 | 192 av 239
Sverige | 64 | 1 476 av 2 320
+Norge | 50 | 33 av 66
# Svenska runstenar efter landskap
Västergötland | 88 | 115 av 131
Östergötland | 69 | 154 av 222
Uppland | 68 | 804 av 1 178
Södermanland | 65 | 236 av 363
+Småland | 40 | 49 av 121
+Gotland | 36 | 15 av 42
+Öland | 27 | 42 av 154
# Svenska runstenar, hela och skadade
Utan förlorade runor | 83 | 642 av 774
+Med förlorade runor | 54 | 834 av 1 546
# Runstenar, tolkade och otolkade
Tolkade | 73 | 1 626 av 2 237
+Otolkade | 46 | 27 av 59
Källa: Samnordisk runtextdatabas 3.1, vikingatida runstenar. En stilgrupp räknas när Rundata anger en annan än "?". Vitkis beräkning.
:::

Mönstret är detsamma var man än skär. Skadan väger tyngst: den som vill datera en skadad sten har stilgruppen till hjälp i ungefär hälften av fallen, för en hel sten i fem av sex. Skillnaden är så stor att slumpen är utesluten som förklaring – sannolikheten att den skulle uppstå av en slump är mindre än en på en kvintiljon. Och den är ingen gåta: ornamentiken sitter på ytan, och det är ytan som vittrar, spricker och muras in. Men följden är densamma oavsett orsak. De stenar som är svårast att läsa är också de som är svårast att datera, och varje kronologisk slutsats vilar på de hela, tolkade stenarna i de välbevarade landskapen.

![Fragmentet U 65 i Spånga kyrka](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/U_65%2C_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG/960px-U_65%2C_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG)
Mörkertalets ansikte: U 65, ett fragment i Spånga kyrka. Ingen ornamentik att stilbestämma, förlorade runor, och av texten återstår bara "… Petar lät(?) …". En av de drygt niohundra. Foto: Jssfrk, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_65,_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG).

Också föremålen utanför runstenarna hör till bilden: gravhällar och berghällar har stilgrupp i 29 fall av hundra, lösa föremål aldrig. Det är väntat – systemet är byggt för runstenar – men det betyder att stilgruppsdatering över huvud taget inte når dit.

## De osynliga är inte som de synliga

Om de niohundra stenarna utan stilgrupp vore ett slumpmässigt urval vore mörkertalet ett irritationsmoment och inget mer: slutsatserna från de synliga stenarna skulle gälla även de osynliga. Det går att pröva. Signaturen – att ristaren skriver sitt namn – är ett drag som inte kräver någon stilbestämning för att räknas, och som forskningen brukar knyta till de senare stilgrupperna.

Här måste skadan först hållas isär: en skadad sten kan ha förlorat både sin ornamentik och sin signatur, och då ser sambandet starkare ut än det är. Vi jämför därför bara hela stenar, utan förlorade runor. Bland Sveriges hela runstenar med stilgrupp är 102 av 642 signerade, 15,9 procent. Hade de hela stenarna utan stilgrupp haft samma blandning av stilar skulle ungefär 16 av hundra vara signerade. I verkligheten är det 8 av 132, 6,1 procent. Så få signaturer bland så många stenar uppstår av slump ungefär en gång på två tusen.

:::chart Andel signerade bland hela svenska runstenar, per stilgrupp
RAK | 4,8 | 7 av 147 hela stenar
Fp | 7,3 | 7 av 96 hela stenar
KB | 5,9 | 1 av 17 hela stenar
Pr1 | 18,9 | 7 av 37 hela stenar
Pr2 | 13,5 | 7 av 52 hela stenar
Pr3 | 25,6 | 21 av 82 hela stenar
Pr4 | 28,1 | 39 av 139 hela stenar
Pr5 | 29,4 | 5 av 17 hela stenar
+Utan stilgrupp | 6,1 | 8 av 132 hela stenar
Källa: Samnordisk runtextdatabas 3.1. Bara stenar utan förlorade runor, så att skadan inte förväxlas med stilen.
:::

Stenarna utan stilgrupp signerar alltså som RAK-stenarna, den grupp som räknas som äldst – inte som genomsnittet. Det finns två läsningar, och båda har följder. Antingen är de ostilsatta stenarna inte slumpmässigt spridda i tiden utan väger mot det tidiga – då är de kronologiska kurvor som ritas på de stilsatta stenarna skeva, eftersom en tidig tredjedel saknas. Eller så speglar bortfallet hur stilbestämningarna har gjorts – vilka stenar som blev granskade, avbildade och inpassade – och då är stilgruppernas täckning själv en historisk källa som ingen har läst. Siffrorna kan inte skilja läsningarna åt. Men ingen av dem tillåter att de osynliga stenarna behandlas som om de inte fanns.

## RAK: kategorin av det som saknas

Den tidigaste gruppen, RAK, definieras inte av ett formspråk utan av frånvaron av ett: raka bandändar, inget djurhuvud. Det fungerar i Uppland, där RAK är en liten minoritet omgiven av daterbara grannar. Men se vad kategorin gör med andra bestånd:

:::chart RAK:s andel av de stilsatta runstenarna
Norge | 100 | 33 av 33
Danmark | 95 | 182 av 192
+Småland | 73 | 36 av 49
+Västergötland | 70 | 81 av 115
Södermanland | 12 | 28 av 236
Uppland | 6 | 50 av 804
Källa: Samnordisk runtextdatabas 3.1, vikingatida runstenar med stilgrupp. Vitkis beräkning.
:::

I Danmark är i stort sett varje stilsatt runsten RAK, i Norge varenda en, i Västergötland och Småland tre av fyra. Läses RAK som en datering – ungefär 980 till 1015 i Gräslunds kronologi – blir nästan hela dessa bestånd tidiga per definition, inte per iakttagelse. För Danmark finns oberoende hållpunkter som pekar åt samma håll, men i varje statistisk jämförelse mellan landskapen blir cirkeln sluten: den som räknar "tidiga" och "sena" stenar per region räknar till stor del var djurornamentiken brukades, inte när stenarna restes. Utanför Mälardalen är RAK mindre en datering än en anteckning om att det inte finns något djur att datera.

![Den mindre Jellingstenen](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg/960px-Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg)
Kung Gorms sten i Jelling (DR 41), rest över drottning Thyra, "Danmarks bot": raka bandändar, ingen djurornamentik – RAK. Så ser nästan varje stilsatt dansk runsten ut i databasen. Foto: Ljunie, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg).

## Vad det betyder för forskningens slutsatser

Varje undersökning som sorterar runstenar efter stilgrupp – när signerandet började, när en böneformel kom och försvann, hur korsen spred sig, vår egen statistik inräknad – gäller i själva verket de två tredjedelar av runstenarna som har en stilgrupp, och den tredjedelen är vald av bevarandet, tolkningen och geografin. Det gör inte slutsatserna fel, men det gör dem villkorade på ett sätt som sällan skrivs ut.

Det enklaste botemedlet kostar en rad: att redovisa täckningen tillsammans med slutsatsen. "Bland de stilsatta stenarna" är en annan utsaga än "bland stenarna", och läsaren bör få veta vilken som görs – med antal: hur många stenar som bär kurvan, och hur många som står utanför den. Vi har börjat göra det i våra egna artiklar, och mönstret i den här artikeln är skälet.

## Mörkertalet kan tändas

Det går att göra mer än att redovisa. Tre lampor finns redan:

- **Seriation på textens och innehållets drag.** Vi har ordnat Upplands runstenar efter språkdrag, formler och innehåll, utan att använda ornamentiken som indata, och prövat ordningen mot de stilsatta stenarna: den följer Gräslunds kronologi med rangkorrelationen 0,543 och skattar styldaterade stenars tid med ett medelfel på 21 år, mot 25 om man gissar medelåret. Rangkorrelationen betyder att ordningen till god del är rätt även när årtalen är osäkra; sambandet står kvar inom enskilda härader. Vinsten är att metoden inte behöver något djur: av Upplands 374 runstenar utan stilgrupp får 317 en tidsplacering, med breda men redovisade osäkerheter. Placeringarna visas sten för sten i Vitkis forskningsvy.
- **Textmodellens datering.** Sannolikhetsmodellen i Vitki, som [läser och fyller runföljder](/artiklar/hur-spraklik-ar-en-runfoljd), daterar också: i korsvaliderade prov träffar den rätt århundrade för 58,5 procent av runstenarna, och i 94,8 fall av hundra ligger den högst en epok fel. Det är grovt jämfört med stilgruppernas decennier – men det är en datering som når varje sten med läsbar text, även de niohundra i mörkret.
- **Det forskningen redan vet men databasen inte rymmer.** I stilfältet skymtar bedömningar som aldrig blev regelrätta poster: hänvisningar till muntliga uppgifter och tryckta supplement, och 73 stenar bär sin stilgrupp med frågetecken. Litteraturen vet mer än databasen. Att samla in stilbedömningar ur Sveriges runinskrifter och senare granskningar till databasens stilfält vore det billigaste enskilda sättet att krympa mörkertalet på riktigt.

![Seriationen av språk och innehåll](/figurer/c1005641fa017cc1.webp)
Seriationsdiagrammet bakom den första lampan. Varje rad är ett drag i text eller innehåll, varje kolumn en tiondel av Upplandsstenarna i seriationens ordning från tidigt till sent: böner och stungna runor tänds, äldre stavningar släcks – och ordningen är byggd utan ornamentiken. Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys i R (chronology.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

## Det siffrorna inte säger

- **Mörkertalet är databasens, inte forskningens.** Vi mäter Rundatas stilfält. Stilbedömningar kan finnas i litteraturen utan att stå där – men varje undersökning som bygger på databasen, vår egen inräknad, ärver ändå just det här bortfallet.
- **Signaturjämförelsen har två läsningar.** Att hela stenar utan stilgrupp signerar som de äldsta kan betyda att de är tidiga, eller att stilbestämmandet valt bort en viss sorts stenar. Våra tal skiljer inte läsningarna åt; det kräver att de ostilsatta stenarna dateras på annan väg.
- **Seriationen är prövad i Uppland.** Utanför Uppland vet vi ännu inte hur väl textens drag bär en tidsordning; inom ristare är sambandet svagare, som väntat när en ristares verksamma år är få.
- **Stilgrupp med frågetecken räknas som stilgrupp.** Vi räknar generöst: även osäkra bestämningar står på ljussidan. Mörkertalet är alltså snarare under- än överskattat.

## Så gjorde vi

- **Underlaget:** alla vikingatida inskrifter i Samnordisk runtextdatabas (3.1, 2018). Runsten är det Rundata kallar runsten eller fragment av runsten; en stilgrupp räknas när stilfältet anger något annat än "?". Skadad betyder förlorade runor eller förlorad text i Rundatas läsning. Signerad betyder att Rundata anger ristaren som signerad (S), inte bara attribuerad.
- **Testerna:** skillnaderna i stilgruppstäckning och signering är prövade med Fishers exakta test, och signeringen bland de ostilsatta mot den väntade andelen med ett exakt binomialtest; alla jämförelser av signering gäller enbart hela stenar. Seriationens validering är korsvaliderad mot de styldaterade stenarna (leave-one-out), med robusthetsprov utan kors, utan utlandsfärdsstenar, utan föränderliga språkdrag samt inom härader och ristare.
- **Skripten:** utdata/sprakprov/stilgrupper.py och utdata/sprakprov/morkertal.py i [kodförrådet](https://github.com/Precatio/runes); seriationen i r/chronology.R. Alla tal i artikeln läses ur skriptens utdata med automatiska kontroller.

:::box Det viktigaste i korthet
- En tredjedel av Sveriges runstenar kan inte stildateras – och de är inte ett slumpmässigt urval. Mörkertalet har ett mönster.
- Hela, välbevarade stenar utan stilgrupp signeras lika sällan som stenarna i den enklaste stilen, RAK. Det tyder på att den odaterade massan domineras av just de enkla stenarna – inte av skadade exemplar av alla sorter.
- Slutsatser som bara bygger på stildaterade stenar lutar sig därmed mot de påkostade och välbevarade, och kan överskatta hur vanligt det ornamentala var.
- Den billigaste boten är dokumentation: många stenar saknar stilgrupp för att ingen har bedömt dem, inte för att ornamentiken är borta.
:::

## Källor

- Samnordisk runtextdatabas (Rundata), Institutionen för nordiska språk, Uppsala universitet. Open Database License.
- Gräslund, A.-S. 2006. Dating the Swedish Viking-Age rune stones on stylistic grounds. I: M. Stoklund m.fl. (red.), *Runes and their Secrets: Studies in Runology*. Köpenhamn: Museum Tusculanum Press, s. 117–139.
- Källström, M. 2007. *Mästare och minnesmärken. Studier kring vikingatida runristare och skriftmiljöer i Norden*. Stockholm: Stockholms universitet.
posts.title_en: The style groups' dark number
posts.summary_en: Runestones are dated by their ornament, yet more than a third of all runestones lack a style group in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database – and the loss is not random. The damaged, the uninterpreted and the stones outside the Mälaren valley and Västergötland drop out most often. We show that the invisible stones do not behave like the visible ones either, that the category RAK makes whole corpora early by definition, and how the dark number can be lit.
posts.body_en:
When Anne-Sofie Gräslund sorted the runestones by the shape of their rune bands and animal ornament, research gained perhaps its sharpest tool: a runestone can be dated to within a few decades without a single year in its text. The style groups today carry much of what we believe we know about the end of the Viking Age – when the carvers began to sign, when the prayers arrived, how the cross spread.

But a tool only sees what lies in its light. This article asks the question that is rarely asked: which runestones do the style groups see – and which stand in the dark? The answer is that more than every third runestone lacks a style group in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database, and that the loss is not random. The stones that are missing are systematically the damaged, the uninterpreted and the peripheral ones. And they do not behave like the visible ones.

:::box In short
- Of 2 633 Viking-age runestones, 1 701 have a style group in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database. More than nine hundred, 35 per cent, stand outside.
- The loss follows the damage: a whole Swedish runestone has a style group in 83 cases out of a hundred, one with lost runes in 54. That so large a difference should arise by chance is in practice excluded.
- It also follows interpretation and geography: the uninterpreted runestones have a style group in 46 cases out of a hundred against 73 for the interpreted, and Öland, Gotland and Småland lie below half.
- The invisible stones are not like the visible ones: whole runestones without a style group are signed in 6 cases out of a hundred, against 16 among the styled – they sign like the oldest style group.
- The category RAK is defined by something that is missing. Among Denmark's styled runestones 95 out of a hundred are RAK, in Norway every one, in Uppland 6 out of a hundred. Read as a date, whole countries become early by definition.
- The dark number can be lit: a seriation dates 317 of Uppland's 374 runestones without a style group, and the text model hits the right century for 58.5 per cent of runestones in cross-validated tests.
:::

## The tool that dates the animals

Gräslund's system runs from RAK, where the rune band has straight ends and no animal head, through the bird's-eye-view Fp and the cross-band style KB to the profile styles Pr1–Pr5, where the animal is seen from the side and grows ever more slender and elongated. The order has been tested against coin-dated hoards and the stones' internal references, and it holds: when we ourselves test Uppland's runestones by seriation, as we show further down, the traits of text and content follow Gräslund's order by a clear margin. Nothing in this article questions the system. The question is what the system does not see.

![The runestone U 142 at Fällbro](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg/960px-Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg)
U 142 at Fällbro in Täby, in the profile style Pr4 and signed by Öpir. The rune band's animal, its head in profile, is the very basis of the dating. Photo: Potatisodlarn, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upplands_Runinskrifter_142.jpg).

## Who stands in the dark

:::chart Share of runestones with a style group in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database
# By country
Denmark | 80 | 192 of 239
Sweden | 64 | 1 476 of 2 320
+Norway | 50 | 33 of 66
# Swedish runestones by province
Västergötland | 88 | 115 of 131
Östergötland | 69 | 154 of 222
Uppland | 68 | 804 of 1 178
Södermanland | 65 | 236 of 363
+Småland | 40 | 49 of 121
+Gotland | 36 | 15 of 42
+Öland | 27 | 42 of 154
# Swedish runestones, whole and damaged
Without lost runes | 83 | 642 of 774
+With lost runes | 54 | 834 of 1 546
# Runestones, interpreted and uninterpreted
Interpreted | 73 | 1 626 of 2 237
+Uninterpreted | 46 | 27 of 59
Source: Scandinavian Runic-text Database 3.1, Viking-age runestones. A style group counts when Rundata gives one other than "?". Vitki's calculation.
:::

The pattern is the same wherever one cuts. Damage weighs heaviest: whoever wants to date a damaged stone has the style group's help in about half of the cases, for a whole stone in five of six. The difference is so large that chance is excluded as an explanation – the probability that it would arise by chance is less than one in a quintillion. Nor is it a mystery: the ornament sits on the surface, and it is the surface that weathers, cracks and gets walled in. But the consequence is the same whatever the cause. The stones that are hardest to read are also the hardest to date, and every chronological conclusion rests on the whole, interpreted stones in the well-preserved provinces.

![The fragment U 65 in Spånga church](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/U_65%2C_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG/960px-U_65%2C_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG)
The face of the dark number: U 65, a fragment in Spånga church. No ornament to assess, lost runes, and of the text only "… Petar had(?) …" remains. One of the more than nine hundred. Photo: Jssfrk, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_65,_Sp%C3%A5nga_kyrka.JPG).

The objects beyond the runestones belong to the picture too: grave slabs and rock faces have a style group in 29 cases out of a hundred, loose objects never. That is expected – the system is built for runestones – but it means style dating does not reach there at all.

## The invisible are not like the visible

If the nine hundred stones without a style group were a random sample, the dark number would be an annoyance and nothing more: conclusions from the visible stones would hold for the invisible as well. That can be tested. The signature – the carver writing their own name – is a trait that needs no style assessment to be counted, and one research usually ties to the later style groups.

The damage must first be kept apart: a damaged stone may have lost both its ornament and its signature, and the connection then looks stronger than it is. We therefore compare whole stones only, without lost runes. Among Sweden's whole runestones with a style group, 102 of 642 are signed, 15.9 per cent. Had the whole stones without a style group had the same mix of styles, about 16 in a hundred would be signed. In reality it is 8 of 132, 6.1 per cent. So few signatures among so many stones arise by chance about once in two thousand.

:::chart Share signed among whole Swedish runestones, by style group
RAK | 4.8 | 7 of 147 whole stones
Fp | 7.3 | 7 of 96 whole stones
KB | 5.9 | 1 of 17 whole stones
Pr1 | 18.9 | 7 of 37 whole stones
Pr2 | 13.5 | 7 of 52 whole stones
Pr3 | 25.6 | 21 of 82 whole stones
Pr4 | 28.1 | 39 of 139 whole stones
Pr5 | 29.4 | 5 of 17 whole stones
+No style group | 6.1 | 8 of 132 whole stones
Source: Scandinavian Runic-text Database 3.1. Only stones without lost runes, so that damage is not confused with style.
:::

The stones without a style group thus sign like the RAK stones, the group counted as oldest – not like the average. There are two readings, and both have consequences. Either the unstyled stones are not randomly spread in time but lean early – then the chronological curves drawn on the styled stones are skewed, because an early third is missing. Or the loss reflects how the style assessments were made – which stones were examined, drawn and fitted in – and then the style groups' coverage is itself a historical source that no one has read. The figures cannot tell the readings apart. But neither of them permits treating the invisible stones as if they did not exist.

## RAK: the category of what is missing

The earliest group, RAK, is defined not by a form language but by the absence of one: straight band ends, no animal head. That works in Uppland, where RAK is a small minority surrounded by datable neighbours. But see what the category does to other corpora:

:::chart RAK's share of the styled runestones
Norway | 100 | 33 of 33
Denmark | 95 | 182 of 192
+Småland | 73 | 36 of 49
+Västergötland | 70 | 81 of 115
Södermanland | 12 | 28 of 236
Uppland | 6 | 50 of 804
Source: Scandinavian Runic-text Database 3.1, Viking-age runestones with a style group. Vitki's calculation.
:::

In Denmark virtually every styled runestone is RAK, in Norway every single one, in Västergötland and Småland three of four. If RAK is read as a date – roughly 980 to 1015 in Gräslund's chronology – nearly all of these corpora become early by definition, not by observation. For Denmark there are independent anchors pointing the same way, but in every statistical comparison between regions the circle closes: whoever counts "early" and "late" stones per region is largely counting where animal ornament was practised, not when the stones were raised. Outside the Mälaren valley, RAK is less a date than a note that there is no animal to date.

![The smaller Jelling stone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg/960px-Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg)
King Gorm's stone at Jelling (DR 41), raised over Queen Thyra, "Denmark's adornment": straight band ends, no animal ornament – RAK. Nearly every styled Danish runestone in the database looks like this. Photo: Ljunie, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Smaller_Jelling_stone.jpg).

## What it means for research's conclusions

Every study that sorts runestones by style group – when signing began, when a prayer formula came and went, how the crosses spread, our own statistics included – in fact concerns the two thirds of runestones that have a style group, and that two thirds is selected by preservation, interpretation and geography. That does not make the conclusions wrong, but it makes them conditional in a way that is seldom written out.

The simplest remedy costs one line: reporting the coverage together with the conclusion. "Among the styled stones" is a different statement from "among the stones", and the reader should be told which one is being made – with numbers: how many stones carry the curve, and how many stand outside it. We have begun doing so in our own articles, and the pattern in this article is the reason.

## The dark number can be lit

More can be done than reporting. Three lamps already exist:

- **Seriation on the traits of text and content.** We have ordered Uppland's runestones by language traits, formulas and content, without using the ornament as input, and tested the order against the styled stones: it follows Gräslund's chronology with rank correlation 0.543 and estimates style-dated stones' time with a mean error of 21 years, against 25 if one guesses the mean year. The rank correlation means the order is largely right even where the years are uncertain; the connection stands within individual districts. The gain is that the method needs no animal: of Uppland's 374 runestones without a style group, 317 receive a placement in time, with wide but stated uncertainties. The placements are shown stone by stone in Vitki's research view.
- **The text model's dating.** The probability model in Vitki, which [reads and fills rune sequences](/artiklar/hur-spraklik-ar-en-runfoljd), also dates: in cross-validated tests it hits the right century for 58.5 per cent of the runestones, and in 94.8 cases out of a hundred it is at most one epoch off. That is coarse beside the style groups' decades – but it is a dating that reaches every stone with readable text, including the nine hundred in the dark.
- **What research already knows but the database does not hold.** In the style field one glimpses assessments that never became proper entries: references to oral statements and printed supplements, and 73 stones carry their style group with a question mark. The literature knows more than the database. Collecting style assessments from Sveriges runinskrifter and later examinations into the database's style field would be the cheapest single way to truly shrink the dark number.

![The seriation of language and content](/figurer/c1005641fa017cc1.webp)
The seriation diagram behind the first lamp. Each row is a trait of text or content, each column a tenth of the Uppland stones in the seriation's order from early to late: prayers and dotted runes light up, older spellings fade – and the order is built without the ornament. Source: Vitki's corpus analysis in R (chronology.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Database (ODbL).

## What the figures do not say

- **The dark number is the database's, not research's.** We measure Rundata's style field. Style assessments may exist in the literature without standing there – but every study built on the database, our own included, still inherits exactly this loss.
- **The signature comparison has two readings.** That whole stones without a style group sign like the oldest ones may mean they are early, or that style assessment has passed over a certain kind of stone. Our figures cannot tell the readings apart; that requires dating the unstyled stones by another route.
- **The seriation is tested in Uppland.** Outside Uppland we do not yet know how well the traits of text carry a time order; within carvers the connection is weaker, as expected when a carver's active years are few.
- **A style group with a question mark counts as a style group.** We count generously: even uncertain assessments stand on the lit side. The dark number is thus under- rather than overestimated.

## How we did it

- **The material:** all Viking-age inscriptions in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database (3.1, 2018). A runestone is what Rundata calls a runestone or fragment of one; a style group counts when the style field gives anything other than "?". Damaged means lost runes or lost text in Rundata's reading. Signed means Rundata marks the carver as signed (S), not merely attributed.
- **The tests:** the differences in style-group coverage and signing are tested with Fisher's exact test, and the signing among the unstyled against the expected share with an exact binomial test; all signing comparisons concern whole stones only. The seriation's validation is cross-validated against the style-dated stones (leave-one-out), with robustness checks without crosses, without the voyage stones, without the changing language traits, and within districts and carvers.
- **The scripts:** utdata/sprakprov/stilgrupper.py and utdata/sprakprov/morkertal.py in [the repository](https://github.com/Precatio/runes); the seriation in r/chronology.R. Every figure in the article is read from the scripts' output with automatic checks.

:::box The essentials in brief
- A third of Sweden's runestones cannot be style-dated – and they are not a random sample. The dark figure has a pattern.
- Whole, well-preserved stones without a style group are signed as rarely as the stones in the plainest style, RAK. This suggests the undated mass is dominated by the plain stones – not by damaged specimens of every kind.
- Conclusions built only on style-dated stones therefore lean on the ornate and well-preserved, and may overstate how common the ornamental was.
- The cheapest remedy is documentation: many stones lack a style group because no one has assessed them, not because the ornament is gone.
:::

## Sources

- Scandinavian Runic-text Database (Rundata), Department of Scandinavian Languages, Uppsala University. Open Database License.
- Gräslund, A.-S. 2006. Dating the Swedish Viking-Age rune stones on stylistic grounds. In: M. Stoklund et al. (eds), *Runes and their Secrets: Studies in Runology*. Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum Press, pp. 117–139.
- Källström, M. 2007. *Mästare och minnesmärken. Studier kring vikingatida runristare och skriftmiljöer i Norden*. Stockholm: Stockholm University.
